claim: Neuropeptide signalling systems comprising peptide ligands and cognate receptors are evolutionarily ancient regulators of physiology and behaviour.
source: Neuropeptide signalling systems comprising peptide ligands and cognate receptors are evolutionarily ancient regulators of physiology and behaviour.
evidence: This is a general statement about neuropeptide systems that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Orthologs of vertebrate neuropeptide-Y (NPY) known as neuropeptide-F (NPF) have been identified in protostome invertebrates.
source: Orthologs of vertebrate neuropeptide-Y (NPY) known as neuropeptide-F (NPF) have been identified in protostome invertebrates, whilst prolactin-releasing peptide (PrRP) and short neuropeptide-F (sNPF) have been identified as paralogs of NPY/NPF in vertebrates and protostomes, respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior research in the field, as detailed in the Introduction section.

claim: Prolactin-releasing peptide (PrRP) and short neuropeptide-F (sNPF) have been identified as paralogs of NPY/NPF in vertebrates and protostomes, respectively.
source: Orthologs of vertebrate neuropeptide-Y (NPY) known as neuropeptide-F (NPF) have been identified in protostome invertebrates, whilst prolactin-releasing peptide (PrRP) and short neuropeptide-F (sNPF) have been identified as paralogs of NPY/NPF in vertebrates and protostomes, respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior research in the field, as detailed in the Introduction section.

claim: Analysis of transcriptome/genome sequence data revealed loss of NPY/NPF-type signalling in echinoderms.
source: Analysis of transcriptome/genome sequence data revealed loss of NPY/NPF-type signalling, but orthologs of PrRP-type neuropeptides and sNPF/PrRP-type receptors were identified in echinoderms.
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of sequence data from echinoderms, as described in the Results section.

claim: Orthologs of PrRP-type neuropeptides and sNPF/PrRP-type receptors were identified in echinoderms.
source: Analysis of transcriptome/genome sequence data revealed loss of NPY/NPF-type signalling, but orthologs of PrRP-type neuropeptides and sNPF/PrRP-type receptors were identified in echinoderms.
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of sequence data from echinoderms, as described in the Results section.

claim: The PrRP-type neuropeptide pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2 is a potent ligand for a sNPF/PrRP-type receptor in the starfish Asterias rubens.
source: Furthermore, experimental studies revealed that the PrRP-type neuropeptide pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2 is a potent ligand for a sNPF/PrRP-type receptor in the starfish Asterias rubens.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental receptor assays shown in Figure 5, demonstrating dose-dependent activation with an EC50 of 1.5 × 10−10 M.

claim: PrRP-type and sNPF-type signalling systems are orthologous and originated as a paralog of NPY/NPF-type signalling in Urbilateria.
source: Our findings indicate that PrRP-type and sNPF-type signalling systems are orthologous and originated as a paralog of NPY/NPF-type signalling in Urbilateria.
evidence: This conclusion is based on phylogenetic analysis, sequence comparisons, and experimental validation of ligand-receptor interactions.

claim: The evolutionary origin of over thirty neuropeptide signalling systems has been traced back to the common ancestor of the Bilateria (Urbilateria).
source: Thus, the evolutionary origin of over thirty neuropeptide signalling systems has been traced back to the common ancestor of the Bilateria (Urbilateria) (Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic and comparative studies.

claim: NPY is a 36-residue peptide that was first isolated from the porcine hypothalamus.
source: NPY is a 36-residue peptide that was first isolated from the porcine hypothalamus (Tatemoto et al., 1982; Tatemoto, 1982) but which is also expressed by neurons in many other regions of the nervous system (Adrian et al., 1983; Morris, 1989) and in peripheral organs such as the gut and cardiovascular system (Holzer et al., 2012; Farzi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: NPY is expressed by neurons in many regions of the nervous system and in peripheral organs such as the gut and cardiovascular system.
source: NPY is a 36-residue peptide that was first isolated from the porcine hypothalamus (Tatemoto et al., 1982; Tatemoto, 1982) but which is also expressed by neurons in many other regions of the nervous system (Adrian et al., 1983; Morris, 1989) and in peripheral organs such as the gut and cardiovascular system (Holzer et al., 2012; Farzi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting NPY expression patterns.

claim: NPY is a potent stimulant of food intake in mammals.
source: Accordingly, NPY is pleiotropic (Pedrazzini et al., 2003), although it is most widely known as a potent stimulant of food intake in mammals (Minor et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on NPY's role in feeding behavior.

claim: NPY belongs to a family of related signalling molecules in vertebrates, including peptide YY (PYY) and pancreatic polypeptide (PP), which evolved from a common ancestral peptide by gene/genome duplication.
source: NPY belongs to a family of related signalling molecules in vertebrates, including peptide YY (PYY) and pancreatic polypeptide (PP), which evolved from a common ancestral peptide by gene/genome duplication (Larhammar et al., 1993; Larhammar, 1996; Elphick et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to evolutionary studies of the NPY family.

claim: The sequences of NPY-type peptides are highly conserved across the vertebrates.
source: Furthermore, the sequences of NPY-type peptides are highly conserved across the vertebrates (Larhammar et al., 1993; Larhammar, 1996; Cerdá-Reverter et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative sequence studies.

claim: Prolactin-releasing peptide (PrRP) was first discovered as a ligand for the orphan receptor hGR3.
source: A neuropeptide in vertebrates that is related to NPY/PYY/PP-type peptides is prolactin-releasing peptide (PrRP), which was first discovered as a ligand for the orphan receptor hGR3 (Hinuma et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: PrRP-type receptors are paralogs of NPY/PYY/PP-type receptors.
source: Phylogenetic analysis has revealed that PrRP-type receptors are paralogs of NPY/PYY/PP-type receptors and it has been proposed that PrRP-type signalling originated in the vertebrate lineage (Lagerström et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a phylogenetic analysis study.

claim: Orthologs of vertebrate PrRP-type receptors have been identified in the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae and the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
source: However, more recently, orthologs of vertebrate PrRP-type receptors have been identified in invertebrate deuterostomes - the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae and the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii - indicating that PrRP-type signalling may have originated in a common ancestor of the deuterostomes (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a phylogenetic study.

claim: A PP-like immunoreactive peptide was identified in the platyhelminth Moniezia expansa.
source: An important insight into the evolutionary history of NPY-related peptides was obtained with identification of a PP-like immunoreactive peptide in a protostome invertebrate, the platyhelminth Moniezia expansa (Maule et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: The invertebrate NPY homolog from Moniezia expansa is a 39-residue peptide with the C-terminal tyrosine (Y) substituted with a phenylalanine (F) and was named neuropeptide F (NPF).
source: Sequencing revealed a 39-residue peptide with a similar structure to NPY, but with the C-terminal tyrosine (Y) substituted with a phenylalanine (F). Hence, this invertebrate NPY homolog was named neuropeptide F (NPF) (Maule et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original sequencing study.

claim: NPF-type neuropeptides have been identified in protostome invertebrates including platyhelminths, molluscs, annelids and arthropods.
source: Subsequently, NPF-type neuropeptides have been identified in other protostome invertebrates, including other platyhelminths (Curry et al., 1992), molluscs (Leung et al., 1992; Rajpara et al., 1992), annelids (Veenstra, 2011; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Bauknecht and Jékely, 2015) and arthropods (Brown et al., 1999), and these peptides typically have a conserved C-terminal RPRFamide motif and range in length from 36 to 40 residues (Fadda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to discovery papers in different taxa.

claim: NPF-type peptides typically have a conserved C-terminal RPRFamide motif and range in length from 36 to 40 residues.
source: Subsequently, NPF-type neuropeptides have been identified in other protostome invertebrates, including other platyhelminths (Curry et al., 1992), molluscs (Leung et al., 1992; Rajpara et al., 1992), annelids (Veenstra, 2011; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Bauknecht and Jékely, 2015) and arthropods (Brown et al., 1999), and these peptides typically have a conserved C-terminal RPRFamide motif and range in length from 36 to 40 residues (Fadda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review summarizing structural features of NPF peptides.

claim: Two novel neuropeptides, ARGPQLRLRFamide and APSLRLRFamide, were discovered in the Colorado potato beetle Leptinotarsa decemlineata using antibodies to M. expansa NPF.
source: Interestingly, this resulted in the discovery of two novel neuropeptides, ARGPQLRLRFamide and APSLRLRFamide, in the Colorado potato beetle Leptinotarsa decemlineata (Spittaels et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: The peptides ARGPQLRLRFamide and APSLRLRFamide were renamed as short neuropeptide F (sNPF) because they are much shorter in length than NPF.
source: As these peptides were isolated using antibodies to M. expansa NPF, they were originally referred to as NPF-related peptides. However, because they are much shorter in length than NPF, they were later renamed as short neuropeptide F (sNPF) (Vanden Broeck, 2001) and homologs were identified in other insects (Schoofs et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the naming and subsequent identification papers.

claim: sNPF-type peptides and precursors exhibit too many differences to be considered orthologs of NPY/NPF-type peptides and precursors.
source: Furthermore, alignment of NPY-type peptides and precursors from vertebrates with NPF-type and sNPF-type peptides and precursors from protostomes revealed that whilst NPF-type peptides are clearly orthologs of vertebrate NPY-type peptides, sNPF-type peptides and precursors exhibit too many differences to be considered orthologs of NPY/NPF-type peptides and precursors (Nässel and Wegener, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a comparative analysis study.

claim: Chordate NPY-type and invertebrate NPF-type neuropeptides are orthologous based on similarity-based clustering methods.
source: Further evidence that chordate NPY-type and invertebrate NPF-type neuropeptides are orthologous has been provided by similarity-based clustering methods, showing that the NPY-type and NPF-type precursors form a pan-bilaterian cluster, whereas sNPF-type precursors form a separate cluster (Jékely, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a clustering analysis study.

claim: A receptor for sNPF-type peptides was first identified in Drosophila melanogaster with the deorphanisation of the GPCR CG7395.
source: A receptor for sNPF-type peptides was first identified in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster with the deorphanisation of the GPCR CG7395 (Mertens et al., 2002), which was previously annotated as a homolog of mammalian NPY-type receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original deorphanisation study.

claim: sNPF receptors have been identified in other insects following the initial discovery in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Subsequently, sNPF receptors have been identified in other insects (Chen and Pietrantonio, 2006; Garczynski et al., 2007; Yamanaka et al., 2008; Dillen et al., 2013; Dillen et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2017; Christ et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to receptor identification studies in various insect species.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, overexpression of sNPF increases food intake in both larvae and adults, whilst loss-of-function sNPF-mutants exhibited reduced food intake.
source: For example, in D. melanogaster overexpression of sNPF increases food intake both in larvae and adults, whilst loss-of-function sNPF-mutants exhibited reduced food intake (Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a functional study in Drosophila.

claim: An expanded family of neuropeptide receptors in C. elegans that had originally been annotated as NPY/NPF-type receptors were found to be orthologs of insect sNPF-receptors.
source: Thus, an expanded family of neuropeptide receptors in the nematode C. elegans that had originally been annotated as NPY/NPF-type receptors (Cardoso et al., 2012) were found to be orthologs of insect sNPF-receptors (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original annotation and the phylogenetic reclassification studies.

claim: sNPF-type peptides and a cognate receptor have been characterised in the bivalve mollusc Crassostrea gigas.
source: Subsequently, sNPF-type peptides and a cognate receptor have been characterised in the bivalve mollusc Crassostrea gigas, confirming the occurrence of this signalling system in the lophotrochozoan branch of the protostomes (Bigot et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a characterization study in oysters.

claim: NPY/NPF receptor-related proteins occur in the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of bilaterian G-protein coupled neuropeptide receptors has demonstrated the occurrence of NPY/NPF receptor-related proteins in ambulacrarians – the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a phylogenetic analysis study.

claim: The precursor of a putative NPY/NPF-type peptide was identified in Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
source: Furthermore, the precursor of a putative NPY/NPF-type peptide was identified in S. kowalevskii (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies identifying the precursor.

claim: A candidate NPY/NPF-type precursor has been identified in the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae.
source: A candidate NPY/NPF-type precursor has also been identified in the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae, but an NPY/NPF-type receptor has yet to be identified in this species (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies identifying the precursor.

claim: A family of neuropeptide precursor-type proteins in echinoderms contain a peptide that shares sequence similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides.
source: A more recent finding was the discovery of a family neuropeptide precursor-type proteins in echinoderms that contain a peptide that shares sequence similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides (Zandawala et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a discovery study.

claim: The sequence of a transcript encoding the precursor of an NPY-like neuropeptide has been reported previously based on analysis of neural transcriptome sequence data from the starfish A. rubens.
source: The sequence of a transcript (contig 1060225; GenBank accession number MK033631.1) encoding the precursor of an NPY-like neuropeptide has been reported previously based on analysis of neural transcriptome sequence data from the starfish A. rubens (Zandawala et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous transcriptome study and a GenBank accession number.

claim: A cDNA encoding the A. rubens NPY-like neuropeptide precursor was cloned and sequenced, revealing an open reading frame encoding a 108-residue protein comprising a predicted 19-residue signal peptide, a 23-residue NPY-like peptide sequence with an N-terminal glutamine residue and a C-terminal glycine residue, followed by a putative monobasic cleavage site.
source: Here, a cDNA encoding this precursor was cloned and sequenced, revealing that the open reading frame encodes a 108-residue protein comprising a predicted 19-residue signal peptide, a 23-residue NPY-like peptide sequence with an N-terminal glutamine residue and a C-terminal glycine residue, followed by a putative monobasic cleavage site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental cloning and sequencing data, with results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Analysis of radial nerve cord extracts using mass spectrometry revealed the presence of a peptide with the structure pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2.
source: Analysis of radial nerve cord extracts using mass spectrometry (LC-MS-MS) revealed the presence of a peptide with the structure pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2, showing that the N-terminal glutamine and C-terminal glycine in the precursor peptide are post-translationally converted to a pyroglutamate residue and an amide group, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The N-terminal glutamine and C-terminal glycine in the precursor peptide are post-translationally converted to a pyroglutamate residue and an amide group, respectively.
source: Analysis of radial nerve cord extracts using mass spectrometry (LC-MS-MS) revealed the presence of a peptide with the structure pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2, showing that the N-terminal glutamine and C-terminal glycine in the precursor peptide are post-translationally converted to a pyroglutamate residue and an amide group, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on mass spectrometry data showing post-translational modifications.

claim: The A. rubens neuropeptide and orthologs from other echinoderms share sequence similarity with both PrRP-type neuropeptides and NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides.
source: Alignment of the sequences of the A. rubens neuropeptide and orthologs from other echinoderms with related peptides in other taxa revealed that they share sequence similarity with both PrRP-type neuropeptides (Figure 1A) and with NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: The echinoderm peptides comprise 22–25 residues and are similar in length to vertebrate PrRPs, which are 20–31 residues as full-length peptides.
source: However, the echinoderm peptides comprise 22–25 residues and are similar in length to vertebrate PrRPs, which are 20–31 residues as full-length peptides and in some species can occur as N-terminally truncated peptides due the presence of a monobasic cleavage site (Hinuma et al., 1998; Tachibana and Sakamoto, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence length comparisons and is supported by citations to studies on PrRP structure.

claim: NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides are longer peptides ranging in length from 36 to 40 residues.
source: This contrasts with NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides, which are longer peptides ranging in length from 36 to 40 residues (Fadda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on NPY/NPF peptide structure.

claim: Novel neuropeptides that share sequence similarity with the echinoderm neuropeptides and with vertebrate PrRPs were identified in the hemichordate S. kowalevskii and the cephalochordate B. floridae.
source: Furthermore, by analysing sequence data from the hemichordate S. kowalevskii and the cephalochordate B. floridae, here we identified novel neuropeptides that share sequence similarity with the echinoderm neuropeptides and with vertebrate PrRPs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and alignment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The echinoderm peptides lack two proline (P) residues that are a conserved feature of the N-terminal region of many NPY/NPF-type peptides.
source: Contrastingly, the echinoderm peptides lack two proline (P) residues that are a conserved feature of the N-terminal region of many NPY/NPF-type peptides, with the exception of some peptides that have only one of these proline residues and a peptide in the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae that has neither (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Four residues (tyrosine, leucine, tyrosine, and isoleucine) are highly conserved in bilaterian NPY/NPF-type peptides and have been shown to be important for the formation of the three-dimensional structure in vertebrate NPY-type peptides.
source: Furthermore, there are four other residues that are highly conserved in bilaterian NPY/NPF-type peptides - tyrosine (Y), leucine (L), tyrosine (Y), and isoleucine (I) residues, which are marked with arrowheads in Figure 1B. These residues have been shown to be important for the formation of the three-dimensional structure in vertebrate NPY-type peptides (Blundell et al., 1981; Glover et al., 1983; Glover et al., 1984; Allen et al., 1987), so these residues may likewise be important for NPF receptor activation and bioactivity.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence conservation analysis and is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: None of the four conserved residues important for NPY/NPF structure are present in the echinoderm peptides.
source: Importantly, none of these residues are present in the echinoderm peptides.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All but one of the six conserved residues in NPY/NPF-type peptides are present in a peptide from the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
source: It is noteworthy, however, that all but one of the aforementioned six conserved residues in NPY/NPF-type peptides are present in a peptide from a species belonging to a sister phylum of the echinoderms – the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii (Figure 1B; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1B and is supported by citations.

claim: A common characteristic of echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes and chordate PrRP genes is the presence of an intron that interrupts the coding sequence at a position corresponding to the N-terminal or central region of the peptides.
source: This revealed that a common characteristic is the presence of an intron that interrupts the coding sequence at a position corresponding to the N-terminal or central region of the echinoderm PrRP-like peptides and vertebrate PrRPs.
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes and vertebrate PrRP genes, the intron interrupts the coding sequence in the same frame, at a position between the first and second nucleotide of the interrupted codon (a phase one intron).
source: Furthermore, in echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes and vertebrate PrRP genes the intron interrupts the coding sequence in the same frame, at a position between the first and second nucleotide of the interrupted codon (a phase one intron), which is denoted by +1 in Figure 2.
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Genes encoding novel precursors of PrRP-like peptides in S. kowalevskii and B. floridae also have a phase one intron.
source: Genes encoding novel precursors of PrRP-like peptides in S. kowalevskii and B. floridae also have a phase one intron.
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of a conserved intron in the same frame in echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes, the two S. kowalevskii PrRP-like peptide genes and chordate PrRP-type genes supports the hypothesis that the echinoderm and hemichordate PrRP-like peptides are orthologs of chordate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
source: The presence of a conserved intron in the same frame in echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes, the two S. kowalevskii PrRP-like peptide genes and chordate PrRP-type genes supports our hypothesis that the echinoderm and hemichordate PrRP-like peptides are orthologs of chordate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene structure conservation analysis.

claim: A conserved feature of NPY/NPF genes is an intron that interrupts the coding sequence for NPY/NPF-type peptides, with the intron located between the second and third nucleotide of the codon for the arginine residue of the C-terminal RF or RY dipeptide.
source: Previous studies have reported that a conserved feature of NPY/NPF genes is an intron that interrupts the coding sequence for NPY/NPF-type peptides, with the intron located between the second and third nucleotide of the codon for the arginine residue of the C-terminal RF or RY dipeptide (Mair et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous gene structure study.

claim: In echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes, the intron does not interrupt the codon for the arginine of the C-terminal RF or RY motif, but instead is located between the first and second nucleotide of the codon for a residue located in the N-terminal or central regions of echinoderm PrRP-like peptides.
source: Thus, it does not interrupt the codon for the arginine of the C-terminal RF or RY motif, but instead it is located between the first and second nucleotide of the codon for a residue located in the N-terminal or central regions of echinoderm PrRP-like peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Typically in NPY/NPF genes there is another intron that interrupts the coding sequence in the C-terminal region of the precursor protein, whereas in the echinoderm PrRP-like peptide precursor genes the coding sequence for the C-terminal region of the precursor protein is not interrupted by an intron.
source: Another difference is that typically in NPY/NPF genes there is another intron that interrupts the coding sequence in the C-terminal region of the precursor protein, whereas in the echinoderm PrRP-like peptide precursor genes the coding sequence for the C-terminal region of the precursor protein is not interrupted by an intron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A transcript (contig 1120879) encoding a 386-residue protein was identified as the best hit when using NPY-type, NPF-type, PrRP-type and sNPF-type receptors as queries for similarity-based analysis of A. rubens neural transcriptome sequence data.
source: Using receptor sequences of H. sapiens NPY-type, D. melanogaster NPF-type, H. sapiens PrRP-type and D. melanogaster sNPF-type receptors as queries for similarity-based analysis of A. rubens neural transcriptome sequence data, a transcript (contig 1120879) encoding a 386-residue protein was identified as the best hit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on BLAST analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: Homologs of the A. rubens protein encoded by contig 1120879 were identified in other echinoderms including the starfish A. planci, the sea urchin S. purpuratus and the sea cucumber A. japonicus.
source: Furthermore, homologs of the A. rubens protein encoded by contig 1120879 were also identified in other echinoderms for which genome sequences have been obtained, including the starfish A. planci, the sea urchin S. purpuratus and the sea cucumber A. japonicus, and importantly no other NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors were identified in these species.
evidence: This claim is based on BLAST analysis of genome data from multiple echinoderm species.

claim: No other NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors were identified in the echinoderms A. planci, S. purpuratus and A. japonicus.
source: Furthermore, homologs of the A. rubens protein encoded by contig 1120879 were also identified in other echinoderms for which genome sequences have been obtained, including the starfish A. planci, the sea urchin S. purpuratus and the sea cucumber A. japonicus, and importantly no other NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors were identified in these species.
evidence: This claim is based on comprehensive BLAST analysis of genome data.

claim: Cluster-based analysis using CLANS revealed three main clusters: a cluster comprising the outgroup receptors (tachykinin/luqin), a cluster comprising NPY/NPF-type receptors, and a cluster comprising sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors.
source: This analysis revealed three main clusters: 1. a cluster comprising the outgroup receptors (tachykinin/luqin), 2. a cluster comprising NPY/NPF-type receptors and 3. a cluster comprising sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors.
evidence: This claim is based on CLANS clustering analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The echinoderm receptors showed stronger connections with the sNPF/PrRP receptor cluster than with the NPY/NPF receptor cluster in CLANS analysis.
source: Interestingly, the echinoderm receptors showed stronger connections with the sNPF/PrRP receptor cluster (Figure 3, black square) than with the NPY/NPF receptor cluster.
evidence: This claim is based on CLANS clustering analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors are orthologous based on cluster-based analysis of receptor sequences.
source: These findings indicate that sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors are orthologous, as has been proposed previously based on cluster-based analysis of receptor sequences (Jékely, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on CLANS analysis and is supported by a citation to a previous clustering study.

claim: NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors in echinoderms are not orthologs of NPY/NPF-type receptors but are orthologs of sNPF/PrRP-type receptors.
source: Furthermore, these findings indicate that NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors in echinoderms are not orthologs of NPY/NPF-type receptors but are orthologs of sNPF/PrRP-type receptors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from CLANS clustering analysis.

claim: The lines linking the echinoderm receptors and nematode sNPF-type receptors with other sNPF/PrRP-type receptors in CLANS are quite long, which is indicative of sequence divergence.
source: However, it is noteworthy that the lines linking the echinoderm receptors and nematode sNPF-type receptors with other sNPF/PrRP-type receptors in CLANS are quite long (Figure 3), which is indicative of sequence divergence.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of CLANS clustering results shown in Figure 3.

claim: In phylogenetic analysis using the maximum likelihood method, the echinoderm receptors are positioned within a branch comprising NPY/NPF-type, PrRP-type and sNPF-type receptors.
source: This revealed that the echinoderm receptors are positioned within a branch of the phylogenetic tree that comprises NPY/NPF-type, PrRP-type and sNPF-type receptors, with the other receptor types included in the analysis occupying an outgroup position (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is based on maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The echinoderm receptors are positioned in a clade comprising sNPF-type receptors, with bootstrap support of >90%.
source: More specifically, the echinoderm receptors are positioned in a clade comprising sNPF-type receptors, with bootstrap support of >90%, indicating that the echinoderm receptors are orthologs of protostome sNPF-type receptors.
evidence: This claim is based on maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis with bootstrap support shown in Figure 4.

claim: sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors do not form a monophyletic clade in the phylogenetic tree.
source: However, it is noteworthy that sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors do not form a monophyletic clade as would be expected for orthologous receptors.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of the phylogenetic tree structure in Figure 4.

claim: The lack of monophyly between sNPF-type and PrRP-type receptors may be a consequence of sequence divergence in the echinoderm and nematode sNPF/PrRP-type receptors.
source: This may be a consequence of sequence divergence in the echinoderm and nematode sNPF/PrRP-type receptors that is reflected in the long branches leading to these receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the phylogenetic tree topology.

claim: There is a long branch leading to the echinoderm receptor clade in the phylogenetic tree.
source: Accordingly, it is noteworthy that in the phylogenetic tree (Figure 4) there is a long branch leading to the echinoderm receptor clade and likewise nematode sNPF-type receptors also have long branches (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of branch lengths in the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sequence identity between echinoderm PrRP-type peptides and protostome sNPF-type peptides is restricted to a few residues in the C-terminal regions of the peptides.
source: This revealed that sequence identity is restricted to a few residues in the C-terminal regions of the peptides and, furthermore, the echinoderm PrRP-type peptides are much longer than protostome sNPF-type peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The echinoderm PrRP-type peptides are much longer than protostome sNPF-type peptides.
source: This revealed that sequence identity is restricted to a few residues in the C-terminal regions of the peptides and, furthermore, the echinoderm PrRP-type peptides are much longer than protostome sNPF-type peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence length comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protostome sNPF-type neuropeptide precursors typically give rise to multiple sNPF-type peptides, whereas echinoderm PrRP-type precursors contain a single PrRP-type neuropeptide that is located adjacent to the signal peptide.
source: Another difference is that protostome sNPF-type neuropeptide precursors typically give rise to multiple sNPF-type peptides, whereas echinoderm PrRP-type precursors are similar to chordate PrRP-type precursors in containing a single PrRP-type neuropeptide that is located adjacent to the signal peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of precursor structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Comparison of the exon/intron structure of the genes encoding PrRP-type precursors in echinoderms and sNPF-type precursors in protostomes revealed limited similarity.
source: Accordingly, comparison of the exon/intron structure of the genes encoding PrRP-type precursors in echinoderms and sNPF-type precursors in protostomes also revealed limited similarity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Analysis of the sequence of Ar-sNPF/PrRPR using Protter revealed seven predicted transmembrane domains.
source: Analysis of the sequence of Ar-sNPF/PrRPR using Protter revealed seven predicted transmembrane domains, as expected for a GPCR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of protein structure shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ArPrRP at a concentration of 10−5 M triggers luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells that were approximately five times the background luminescence.
source: This revealed that ArPrRP at a concentration of 10−5 M triggers luminescence responses (defined as 100%) in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells that were approximately five times the background luminescence detected with the assay media used to dissolve the peptide (Figure 5A), demonstrating that ArPrRP acts as a ligand for the receptor.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental receptor assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ArPrRP acts as a ligand for the Ar-sNPF/PrRPR receptor.
source: This revealed that ArPrRP at a concentration of 10−5 M triggers luminescence responses (defined as 100%) in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells that were approximately five times the background luminescence detected with the assay media used to dissolve the peptide (Figure 5A), demonstrating that ArPrRP acts as a ligand for the receptor.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental receptor assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ArPrRP induced dose-dependent luminescence in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells with a half-maximal response concentration (EC50) of 1.5 × 10−10 M.
source: Furthermore, ArPrRP induced dose-dependent luminescence in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells with a half-maximal response concentration (EC50) of 1.5 × 10−10 M (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No response to ArPrRP was observed in CHO-K1 cells transfected with the vector alone.
source: Importantly, no response to ArPrRP was observed in CHO-K1 cells transfected with the vector alone, demonstrating that the signal observed in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells exposed to ArPrRP can be attributed to activation of the transfected receptor (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on negative control experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C-terminal pentapeptide of ArPrRP (LNPRFamide) did not induce luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells.
source: However, this peptide did not induce luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental receptor assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The 22-residue amidated peptide ArPrRP is the natural ligand for Ar-sNPF/PrRPR in A. rubens.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the 22-residue amidated peptide ArPrRP is the natural ligand for Ar-sNPF/PrRPR in A. rubens.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing that the full-length peptide activates the receptor while the truncated peptide does not.

claim: The A. rubens luqin-type neuropeptide ArLQ did not induce luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells.
source: The A. rubens luqin-type neuropeptide ArLQ also did not induce luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells, demonstrating the selectivity of Ar-sNPF/PrRPR for ArPrRP as a ligand (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental receptor assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NPY/NPF-type neuropeptide signalling has been lost in the phylum Echinodermata.
source: Therefore, we conclude that NPY/NPF-type neuropeptide signalling has been lost in the phylum Echinodermata (Figure 6).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the absence of NPY/NPF-type peptides and receptors in echinoderm sequence data.

claim: Loss of NPY/NPF-type signalling has been reported in urochordates.
source: This is a noteworthy because, to the best of our knowledge, the only other taxon in which loss of NPY/NPF-type signalling has been reported are the urochordates, a sub-phylum of the phylum Chordata (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous phylogenetic study.

claim: The peptide MDANAFRMSFamide has been shown to activate the C. elegans receptor NPR-11.
source: Here, our phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4) indicates that there are two C. elegans receptors that are orthologs of NPY/NPF-type receptors: NPR-12, which is an orphan receptor, and NPR-11, which has been shown to be activated by the peptide MDANAFRMSFamide (Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a receptor deorphanisation study.

claim: The peptide MDANAFRMSFamide shares little sequence similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides from other bilaterians.
source: However, this peptide shares little sequence similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides from other bilaterians.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Receptor assays for NPR-11 only showed activation at peptide concentrations of 10 and 30 µM, which are high when compared to other NPY/NPF-type receptors that are typically activated by ligands in the nanomolar range.
source: Furthermore, receptor assays only showed activation at peptide concentrations of 10 and 30 µM (Chalasani et al., 2010), which are high when compared to other NPY/NPF-type receptors that are typically activated by ligands in the nanomolar range (Bard et al., 1995; Lundell et al., 1997; Garczynski et al., 2002; Saberi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of receptor activation data from multiple cited studies.

claim: The mature peptide derived from the C. elegans protein FLP-27 may be an ortholog of NPY/NPF-type peptides based on similarity-based sequence alignments.
source: Recently, based on similarity-based sequence alignments, it has been suggested that the mature peptide derived from the C. elegans protein FLP-27 may be an ortholog of NPY/NPF-type peptides (Fadda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a sequence analysis study.

claim: The gene encoding the FLP-27 precursor has the characteristic structure of NPY/NPF-type genes, with an intron interrupting the codon for the C-terminal arginine of the NPF-type peptide sequence.
source: Here, our analysis of the structure of the gene encoding the FLP-27 precursor has revealed that it has the characteristic structure of NPY/NPF-type genes, with an intron interrupting the codon for the C-terminal arginine of the NPF-type peptide sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NPY/NPF-type peptide derived from the FLP-27 precursor protein is likely to act as a ligand for the NPR-11 and/or NPR-12 receptors.
source: Thus, based on our analysis of C. elegans sequence data, we conclude that the NPY/NPF-type peptide derived from the FLP-27 precursor protein is likely to act as a ligand for the NPR-11 and/or NPR-12 receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from gene structure and receptor phylogeny analysis.

claim: The echinoderm neuropeptides share sequence similarity with vertebrate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
source: If the echinoderm NPY-like peptides are not orthologs of NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides, then what are they? Here we show that these peptides share sequence similarity with vertebrate PrRP-type neuropeptides (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The coding sequence for the echinoderm neuropeptides is interrupted by an intron in the phase one frame, a feature that is also characteristic of genes encoding vertebrate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the structure of the genes encoding the echinoderm neuropeptides revealed that the coding sequence for the neuropeptides is interrupted by an intron in the phase one frame, a feature that is also a characteristic of genes encoding vertebrate PrRP-type neuropeptides (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The echinoderm neuropeptides are orthologs of vertebrate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
source: These findings indicate that the echinoderm neuropeptides are orthologs of vertebrate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
evidence: This conclusion is based on sequence similarity and gene structure conservation.

claim: A previous cluster-based analysis of receptor sequence data has reported that vertebrate PrRP-type receptors cluster with protostome sNPF-type receptors, indicating that these receptors may be orthologous.
source: Accordingly, a previous cluster-based analysis of receptor sequence data has reported that vertebrate PrRP-type receptors cluster with protostome sNPF-type receptors, indicating that these receptors may be orthologous (Jékely, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous clustering study.

claim: The echinoderm receptors are orthologs of PrRP/sNPF-type receptors but have undergone sequence divergence.
source: This suggests that the echinoderm receptors are orthologs of PrRP/sNPF-type receptors but have undergone sequence divergence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the long connection lines in CLANS analysis.

claim: A group of sNPF-type receptors in the nematode C. elegans appears to be similarly divergent with respect to other sNPF/PrRP-type receptors.
source: Interestingly, a group of sNPF-type receptors in the nematode C. elegans appears to be similarly divergent with respect to other sNPF/PrRP-type receptors (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of CLANS clustering results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The discovery of PrRP/sNPF-type signalling in echinoderms has provided a unique opportunity to speculate on the ancestral characteristics of this signalling system in Urbilateria.
source: The discovery of PrRP/sNPF-type signalling in echinoderms has provided a unique opportunity to speculate on the ancestral characteristics of this signalling system in Urbilateria.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for evolutionary reconstruction.

claim: PrRP-type peptides and precursors may more closely resemble the ancestral characteristics of the PrRP/sNPF type signalling system in Urbilateria.
source: Based on these observations, we propose that PrRP-type peptides and precursors may more closely resemble the ancestral characteristics of the PrRP/sNPF type signalling system in Urbilateria.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on comparative analysis of peptide and precursor structures.

claim: The common ancestor of the paralogous NPY/NPF-type and PrRP/sNPF-type neuropeptide precursors may have been similar to NPY/NPF-type precursors with respect to peptide, precursor and gene structure.
source: Furthermore, we speculate that the common ancestor of the paralogous NPY/NPF-type and PrRP/sNPF-type neuropeptide precursors may have been similar to NPY/NPF-type precursors with respect peptide, precursor and gene structure.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about ancestral characteristics.

claim: Following gene duplication, the ancestral characteristics were retained in the paralog that gave rise to the bilaterian NPY/NPF-type peptides/precursors.
source: Then, following gene duplication, these ancestral characteristics were retained in the paralog that gave rise to the bilaterian NPY/NPF-type peptides/precursors.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary scenario.

claim: The paralog that gave rise to PrRP/sNPF-type signalling diverged from the ancestral condition.
source: In contrast, the paralog that gave rise to PrRP/sNPF-type signalling diverged from the ancestral condition.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary scenario.

claim: In deuterostomes, the PrRP-type peptides/precursors have many NPY/NPF-type characteristics and this reflects less divergence from the proposed ancestral condition.
source: In deuterostomes, the PrRP-type peptides/precursors have many NPY/NPF-type characteristics and we conclude that this reflects less divergence from the proposed ancestral condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative sequence and structure analysis.

claim: In the protostomes, the sNPF-type peptides/precursors exhibit little similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides/precursors and this reflects more divergence from the proposed ancestral condition.
source: Conversely, in the protostomes, the sNPF-type peptides/precursors exhibit little similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides/precursors and we conclude that this reflects more divergence from the proposed ancestral condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative sequence and structure analysis.

claim: The discovery of a PrRP/sNPF-type signalling system in echinoderms has provided a missing link that unites PrRP-type peptides in vertebrates and sNPF-type peptides in protostomes as members of a bilaterian family of neuropeptides.
source: In conclusion, our discovery of a PrRP/sNPF-type signalling system in echinoderms has provided a missing link that unites PrRP-type peptides in vertebrates and sNPF-type peptides in protostomes as members of a bilaterian family of neuropeptides, as illustrated in Figure 6.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data and analyses presented in the study.
